replacement: “Oh, how low that would have been! Gentlemen, do you know, you’re torturing me! All right, I’ll tell you everything. I’ll confess all my infernal wickedness, but only to put you to shame. You’ll be amazed yourselves at the depths of disgrace a jumble of human passions can sink to. You should know that I had that plan myself, the one you just mentioned, prosecutor! Yes, gentlemen, that thought has been in my head all this month too. I was on the point of deciding to go to Katya—I was mean enough for that. But to go to her, to tell her about my treachery, and for that very treachery, to carry it out, to pay for that treachery, to beg money from her, from Katya (to beg, do you hear, to beg), and go straight from her to run away with the other woman, her rival, who hated her and insulted her—to think of it! You must be mad, prosecutor!”

“But that would have been so infamous!” Mitya brought his fist down fiercely on the table. “It would have been filthier than anything! Do you know, she might have given me that money? Yes, she would have given it; she’d certainly have given it, out of revenge, to satisfy her vengeance, to show me her contempt. She has an infernal nature too, and she’s a woman of great wrath. I’d have taken it, oh yes, I’d have taken the money; I’d have taken it, and then for the rest of my life ... oh, God! Forgive me, gentlemen, I’m shouting like this because the thought has been in my mind so recently, only the day before yesterday, that night when I was having all that trouble with Lyagavy, and then all day yesterday, I remember, right up until that happened ...”

They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch had named: Stepan and Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver backed up Trifon Borissovitch’s story without a moment’s doubt. They wrote down with special care Andrey’s report of what Mitya had said to him on the road: “‘Where am I going,’ he says, ‘Dmitri Fyodorovitch, to heaven or to hell? And shall I be forgiven in the next world or not?’”
